body: Valcourt Building Services of Georgia, L.C. had a contract with the owner of a commercial building to provide exterior maintenance, including pressure washing the rooftop cooling-tower fans. BSC Realty Services, LLC managed the building. Valcourt subcontracted the fan cleaning to a maintenance company owned by the worker who was later hurt. In the contract, Valcourt agreed to defend and indemnify both the owner and BSC against injury claims arising from its work or its subcontractors' work. The only exception was liability arising from the sole negligence of the owner or manager.

On October 7, 2021, the worker checked in with the building's engineers, who worked for a BSC affiliate. They confirmed that power to the first fan was off, and he cleaned it. After they confirmed power was off to a second fan, he climbed a ladder, held a blade with one hand and began washing. He heard a click, the fan began to turn, and he fell and was seriously injured. The engineers could shut fans down either through the building automation system or at a locked rooftop electrical room, and there were no written procedures for doing so at the time. Only the electrical room allowed a federal lockout/tagout procedure. The worker's expert testified that cutting power through the automation system alone did not properly de-energize the fan.

The worker sued several defendants, including BSC. BSC filed a third-party claim against Valcourt for breach of contract and indemnification. The trial court granted summary judgment to Valcourt, accepting its argument that any liability arose from the sole negligence of the owner or manager, through the engineers' failure to keep power to the fan cut off. Valcourt also argued that BSC's appeal was untimely. The appeals court disagreed: no civil case disposition form had been filed, so no final judgment was entered under OCGA 9-11-58(b), the order remained interlocutory, and the trial court could vacate and re-enter it.

On the merits, Presiding Judge McFadden's opinion for the Fourth Division found no direct evidence of whether the fan had power when the worker fell. The automation logs had not been kept. The circumstantial evidence pointed both ways. The click suggested power was restored, but other evidence showed the fan makes little or no noise when re-energized, water pressure from a power washer alone can turn the blades, and a co-worker saw the blades slowing after the fall. A jury could reasonably find that water, not electricity, moved the fan. Because of that dispute, Valcourt could not show as a matter of law that the sole-negligence exception applied, so the summary judgment was reversed. The court did not reach BSC's separate argument about Valcourt's training of the worker.
